power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: Malaria parasite genotyping and molecular force of infection inference improves standard malaria intervention efficacy analysis.
Malaria remains a significant public health threat, causing over 600,000 deaths and 250 million clinical cases each year (1).
text.formatted: Malaria remains a significant public health threat, causing over 600,000 deaths and 250 million clinical cases each year <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(1)</ref>.

text.text: The disease burden is greatest in Sub-Saharan Africa, where Plasmodium falciparum is the dominant species of malaria parasite.

Following a decade of stagnating progress in malaria control, new momentum is expected from the recent implementation of the malaria vaccines RTS,S/AS01 and R21/Matrix-M in Africa, primarily aimed at reducing disease burden among young children, and from a recent surge in the development of new countermeasures suitable for wider age groups as well as during pregnancy.

New biomedical interventions in development include next-generation vaccines, long-acting monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) (https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?0mmNwB and long-acting injectable small-molecule drugs (LAIs) (3).
text.formatted: New biomedical interventions in development include next-generation vaccines, long-acting monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) (<ref type="url" target="https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?0mmNwB">2),</ref> and long-acting injectable small-molecule drugs (LAIs) <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(3)</ref>.

text.text: These strategies are intended to complement mosquito vector interventions, which continue to represent the mainstay of malaria control (4).
text.formatted: These strategies are intended to complement mosquito vector interventions, which continue to represent the mainstay of malaria control <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(4)</ref>.

text.text: Traditionally, early-phase clinical trials that are designed to assess the efficacy of candidate malaria interventions in endemic regions have often relied on "time-to-first event" analysis using Cox proportional hazards models.

These may use time-to-first malaria infection (https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?Fb8wuv) based on thick blood smear microscopy (TBS) or PCR-based methods performed on serially sampled blood as primary endpoints (8, 9, 11).
text.formatted: These may use time-to-first malaria infection (<ref type="url" target="https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?Fb8wuv">5-10</ref>) based on thick blood smear microscopy (TBS) or PCR-based methods performed on serially sampled blood as primary endpoints <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(8,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">9,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">11)</ref>.

text.text: The use of time-to-first-event endpoints in malaria intervention trials has several important limitations.
First, TBS and PCR-based methods cannot distinguish new vs. persisting infections.
The approach assumes that time to first infection adequately reflects the overall longitudinal risk of infection during the entire trial period.
Second, censoring participants after their first infection can introduce bias by decreasing the size of the study population and changing its risk profile over time.

For example, individuals in the control arm who are at high risk of infective mosquito bites, such as those living near mosquito breeding sites, are more likely to be infected and censored early in the trial, while those in the intervention arm(s) who are at equally high risk of infective mosquito bites may remain in the at-risk population longer if the intervention is protective.
The control arm is thus expected to become enriched for individuals at lower risk, resulting in an artefactual decline in intervention efficacy over time.

Beyond distorting time-specific efficacy estimates, the time-to-first event approach can bias the composite efficacy metric by violating the proportional hazards and constant risk composition assumptions that underlie Cox models and similar survival regression methods (12, 13).
text.formatted: Beyond distorting time-specific efficacy estimates, the time-to-first event approach can bias the composite efficacy metric by violating the proportional hazards and constant risk composition assumptions that underlie Cox models and similar survival regression methods <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(12,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">13)</ref>.

text.text: The above limitations of time-to-event analysis can be addressed by including parasite genotypic endpoints to distinguish new from persistent infection states and thereby resolve total infection incidence.

This approach enables all participants to remain in the at-risk population throughout the trial follow-up period, allowing for a more complete picture of the infection burden prevented by the intervention.

In addition, strainand allele-level analysis of breakthrough infections can identify parasite polymorphisms linked to intervention 'escape', providing insight into the mechanisms underlying intervention failure.

Here, we explored the utility of including parasite genotypic endpoints in clinical trials of malaria interventions by applying this approach to a previously described phase 2 trial of the long-acting mAb CIS43LS (6, 14).
text.formatted: Here, we explored the utility of including parasite genotypic endpoints in clinical trials of malaria interventions by applying this approach to a previously described phase 2 trial of the long-acting mAb CIS43LS <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(6,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">14)</ref>.

text.text: CIS43LS targets a conserved 'junctional' epitope spanning the N-terminal and central repeat regions of the P. falciparum circumsporozoite protein (PfCSP) (15).
text.formatted: CIS43LS targets a conserved 'junctional' epitope spanning the N-terminal and central repeat regions of the P. falciparum circumsporozoite protein (PfCSP) <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(15)</ref>.

text.text: As previously reported, a single intravenous dose of 40 mg/kg of CIS43LS provided 88.2% protective efficacy against the first P. falciparum infection detected by TBS (https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?Z54Rn3) and 87.4% efficacy against the first infection detected by qRT-PCR (https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?IchNJN) during a six-month malaria season.
text.formatted: As previously reported, a single intravenous dose of 40 mg/kg of CIS43LS provided 88.2% protective efficacy against the first P. falciparum infection detected by TBS (<ref type="url" target="https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?Z54Rn3">6</ref>) and 87.4% efficacy against the first infection detected by qRT-PCR (<ref type="url" target="https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?IchNJN">14</ref>) during a six-month malaria season.

text.text: We re-analyzed this trial using genotypic endpoints generated via PCR amplicon sequencing (AmpSeq) at seven polymorphic P. falciparum targets, estimating the number of distinct strains newly acquired per follow-up visit per participant.
We used the genotypic data to calculate three CIS43LS efficacy estimates.

The first is efficacy against the molecular force of infection (molFOI)https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?vMDBh3 the number of newly acquired parasite strains over time (16) , which we denote as EffmolFOI.
text.formatted: The first is efficacy against the molecular force of infection (molFOI), the number of newly acquired parasite strains over time <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(16)</ref> <ref type="url" target="https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?vMDBh3">,</ref> which we denote as EffmolFOI.

text.text: EffmolFOI is defined as one minus the ratio of incidence of new strains in the treated vs. control arms and incorporates the number of events over follow-up, but does not consider time-to-first event.
The second genotyping-informed estimate is the proportion reduction in the incidence of new malaria infections (where one "infection" may include multiple strains) over the course of follow-up.
We denote this EffIRR for the incidence rate ratio.
The third estimate, EffFH, integrates time to first infection together with the number of strains at first infection, but it does not consider subsequent infection events.
Proposed by Follmann and Huang, this efficacy estimate is defined as the proportional reduction in mean number of strains that develop into a blood-stage infection from an exposure (17).
text.formatted: Proposed by Follmann and Huang, this efficacy estimate is defined as the proportional reduction in mean number of strains that develop into a blood-stage infection from an exposure <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(17)</ref>.

text.text: EffFH is estimated as one minus the product of the Cox-estimated hazard ratio (HR) multiplied by the ratio of the mean number of strains at first infection in treated vs. control arms.
We compare these genotyping-informed efficacy estimates to the time-to-first event-based efficacy estimates previously used to evaluate CIS43LS efficacy in this trial (6, 14).
text.formatted: We compare these genotyping-informed efficacy estimates to the time-to-first event-based efficacy estimates previously used to evaluate CIS43LS efficacy in this trial <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(6,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">14)</ref>.

text.text: These include efficacy calculated as 1 -HR based on thick blood smear microscopy, efficacy as 1 -HR based on qRT-PCR, and efficacy as 1 -risk ratio for the risk of at least one infection detected by qRT-PCR during the follow-up period.

As previously reported, between May 6 and August 6, 2021, 330 healthy adult participants who met eligibility criteria were randomized and received a single IV infusion of normal saline placebo (n=110), or CIS43LS at a dose of 10 mg/kg (n=110) or 40 mg/kg (n=110) (6).
text.formatted: As previously reported, between May 6 and August 6, 2021, 330 healthy adult participants who met eligibility criteria were randomized and received a single IV infusion of normal saline placebo (n=110), or CIS43LS at a dose of 10 mg/kg (n=110) or 40 mg/kg (n=110) <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(6)</ref>.

text.text: Thereafter, dried blood spot (DBS) and TBS samples were collected at 3 to 14-day intervals for 24 weeks and during unscheduled illness visits when malaria was suspected (Fig. 1A).

text.text: Follow-up through the last trial visit was completed by 102 (92.7%) participants who received placebo, 105 (95.5%) who received 10 mg/kg of CIS43LS, and 104 (94.5%) who received 40 mg/kg of CIS43LS.

Seven-locus P. falciparum AmpSeq genotyping (SIMPLseq + Nterm assay, see Materials and Methods) was performed using DNA obtained from DBS collected from 232 participants (70.3% of total study population) during 1,207 study visits, from a total of 5,657 visits with available DBS.
Of these 1,207 visits, 865 (71.7%) showed AmpSeq signal at one or more loci (Fig. 1B).

text.text: Together with the qRT-PCR and TBS data, the AmpSeq data provided longitudinal infection profiles for each study participant.
Fig. 1C provides an example infection profile of a single participant in the placebo arm whose first infection was detected on day 42.

text.text: For this infection, 1 allele was observed at each of the 7 genotyped loci, suggesting the presence of a single parasite strain (i.e. complexity of infection (COI) = 1).

This participant carried the same strain at fluctuating parasitemias until day 138, at which point a symptomatic superinfection consisting of 2 new strains was observed, prompting successful treatment with artemether-lumefantrine (AL).
Data files S1 and S2 provide infection trajectories for each AmpSeq-positive participant, with and without imputation for missing genotype data at AmpSeq-negative timepoints.
The combination of qRT-PCR and AmpSeq data enabled us to track new parasite strain acquisition over the complete follow-up period for each participant (Fig. 2A).

Here we explored the use of P. falciparum genotypic analysis in a clinical trial of a candidate malaria intervention to estimate efficacy and to detect parasite polymorphisms that might escape the intervention.

Specifically, we genotyped P. falciparum infections that were detected in a phase 2 trial of the anti-malaria mAb CIS43LS and compared efficacy estimates based on molFOI to traditional methods that use PCR-or TBS-based infection endpoints and time-to-first infection (HR) analysis.

Overall, we found that parasite genotypic analysis provided a more comprehensive picture of intervention efficacy than is possible with qRT-PCR or TBS microscopy alone, and critically, the genotypic analysis did not reveal associations between breakthrough infections that occurred in CIS43LS recipients and polymorphisms within or near the PfCSP epitope that CIS43LS targets.
We found that the aggregate 6-month CIS43LS efficacy estimates were similar in magnitude and precision when determined by the molFOI method and the standard HR method.

However, when analyzed by month, the precision of efficacy estimates was higher with the molFOI method, and that precision increased with time relative to the HR method as trial participants experienced their first infections and were removed (censored) from the population at risk that contributed to the HR efficacy estimate.

Notably, the lower bound of the 95% confidence interval for protective efficacy remained above 77% by molFOI as opposed to 3% by HR at month 6 in the 40 mg/kg CIS43LS arm, underscoring the ability of molFOI to assess efficacy with greater precision over the entire follow-up period, a feature that could have implications for future trial designs (e.g. smaller sample size) and for improving the accuracy of efficacy predictions beyond the follow-up period.

Importantly, by capturing total infection incidence with molFOI, and not censoring participants after their first infection, the size and risk profile of the study population included in the molFOI efficacy analysis was maintained throughout the follow-up period, a feature precluded by HR analysis that censors participants after their first infection, potentially introducing bias into efficacy estimates.

For example, with HR analysis we found that censoring participants after their first infections resulted in more rapid depletion of participants who were infected at enrollment, a marker of higher infection risk.
The depletion effect was relatively small in this trial and did not bias EffHR estimates.

It will be important to assess the impact of depletion effects in future malaria intervention trials, particularly those involving children who have less acquired immunity to bloodstage malaria and are therefore more likely to experience patent parasitemia and symptomatic malaria earlier in a trial.

text.text: First, for interventions that aim to block sporozoite infection, qRT-PCR offers greatly enhanced sensitivity relative to TBS, and superior sensitivity to genotyping.

Interpretive ambiguities related to the high sensitivity of qRT-PCR, for example distinguishing new infection from recrudescence following drug treatment of baseline parasitemia, may be clarified by genotyping (9).

text.text: Second, the improved precision and potentially reduced bias in efficacy estimation offered by molFOI may warrant genotyping, particularly as new malaria interventions are deployed and clinical trials contend with measuring protection against the backdrop of an escalating standard of care.
Third, genotyping only the first infection (the Follmann-Huang approach) is not advised, because the seasonal timing of first infections may differ systematically between study arms.

Therefore, if a genotypic estimate of molFOI is planned, we recommend genotyping all infected samples collected during followup, ideally with infected samples first identified using qRT-PCR for cost-effectiveness.

In summary, while molecular endpoints of infection such as qRT-PCR and genotyping carry additional costs beyond clinical disease or microscopy-based endpoints, they can uniquely inform whether candidate malaria interventions may support disease elimination by decreasing transmission risk, in addition to reducing clinical disease burden.

text.text: The model treats longitudinal allele observations as outcomes of latent infection states and estimates, via posterior inference, the probability that each observed allele reflects either persistence of an existing strain or acquisition of a new strain.
For each participant timepoint, new allele presences inferred per locus are summarized into an expected number of newly acquired strains.
DINEMITES also estimates the number of distinct infection events for each subject.

An "infection event" is defined as transmission of malaria parasites from a mosquito to a human, potentially involving multiple strains, and is assigned to the sampling timepoint rather than the actual transmission time (expected to have occurred approximately 10 days earlier, based on the P. falciparum incubation period (27)).

text.text: DINEMITES assignment of infection events accounts for the possibility that alleles introduced by a single infection become detectable over several visits due to imperfect detection and temporal variation in parasite density.
At most one infection event is inferred per sampling timepoint, as multiple transmission events occurring within a sampling interval cannot be distinguished.
DINEMITES included imputation for qRT-PCR positive samples with missing genotyping data; 50 augmented datasets were generated including expected new strain counts for each person-timepoint.

text.text: The first two efficacy estimation methods are commonly applied and analyze only the time to first malaria infection, without incorporating data from later samples.
The latter three methods incorporate information obtained from genotyping.
Risk ratio (RR) efficacy, denoted EffRR, is estimated as one minus the risk ratio (1-RR), which is the CIS43LS-induced proportion reduction in probability of malaria infection during follow-up.
In this analysis, malaria infection was defined as qRT-PCR positivity.

Hazard ratio (HR) efficacy, denoted EffHR, against malaria infection is estimated as one minus the hazard ratio (1-HR), which is the CIS43LS-induced proportion reduction in hazard of malaria infection during follow-up.
This measure incorporates information about the time to first infection but does not use information about later infections or number of strains at first infection.
EffHR was calculated both for the hazard of qRT-PCR positivity, and for the hazard of TBS positivity during follow-up.
Follmann-Huang (FH) efficacy, denoted EffFH, is defined as the CIS43LS-induced proportion reduction in number of infecting strains per exposure.
In field trials, we do not observe exposure events of participants, so we cannot calculate mean strains per exposure.

Follmann and Huang demonstrated that under randomization (which ensures similar exposure distributions in the study arms), we can estimate EffFH as where and are mean numbers of strains for observed infections (rather than exposure events) in treated and controls, respectively, and HR is the hazard ratio for time to first observed infection obtained from a Cox model.

The rationale for this is that a treatment that reduces the number of strains per exposure will convert some infections to non-infections (by converting exposure events with non-zero strains to exposure events with zero strains), which pushes back the time to first infection.
This measure incorporates the time to first infection and number of strains present at the first infection.

This is why, although the estimand is one minus the ratio of means, a valid estimator is one minus the HR times the ratio of truncated means, where the truncation excludes all exposures with zero infecting strains as these are unobservable.
Molecular force of infection (molFOI) efficacy, denoted EffmolFOI, is estimated as one minus the incidence of strains per unit time in treated vs. control participants.
This measure incorporates information about the number of strains per participant acquired during follow-up but discards the timing information.
Incidence rate ratio efficacy, denoted EffIRR, is estimated as one minus the incidence of new malaria infections determined by DINEMITES, where one "infection" may include multiple strains.

First, the p_new values of present alleles are summed within each visit, and the visits are 147 partitioned over time into multi-visit chunks separated by local minima in the sums.
Within each chunk whose 148 largest per-visit sum reaches at least 1, the largest p_new value across the alleles and visits in that chunk 149 (typically 1) is added to the infection event count.
The maximum is used because a single infection is 150 evidenced by how confidently at least one allele is new, without summing co-detected alleles from the same 151 infection event.

At each remaining visit in the chunk, the minimum p_new is added to the infection count, 152 crediting additional infection events only to the extent that every allele at that visit appears new and thus 153 avoiding re-counting alleles already attributed via the primary maximum or that were part of the same infection 154 event but were missed in sequencing on the chunk's maximum day.
If no visit in a chunk has a p_new sum of at least 1, the chunk is treated as too weak for a clear infection event.
For each visit in those chunks, the 156 smallest allele p_new among alleles present is recorded, and the largest of those values across the chunk is 157 added as a fractional residual.
